messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 67-year-old married man who worked for decades as a school principal, a role he loved for its order and predictability. That life ended on a rainy Tuesday evening eight months ago, when a driver ran a red light and T-boned Arthur’s sedan at an intersection. The impact spun his car into a utility pole. He remembers the shriek of twisting metal, the sensation of his body being thrown sideways against the seatbelt, and then the silence before the ringing in his ears began. He was trapped for nearly twenty minutes before firefighters cut him free. Physically, he recovered; the bruises faded, the cracked ribs healed. But something else did not.

Now, a car braking too hard on the street outside his home will send Arthur’s heart racing, and he finds himself suddenly back in that spinning vehicle, the smell of gasoline sharp in his nostrils. He cannot put the event into words—when his wife asks what happened, he just shakes his head, because the memory is not a story he can tell; it is a film that plays over and over, and when it plays, he feels like it is happening right now. He has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse, that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place where catastrophe waits at every intersection. What frightens him most is the certainty that somebody else—a better man, a stronger man—would not have gotten into this situation in the first place.

This conviction drives almost everything Arthur does. Because the world is dangerous, he scans for threats constantly. When something takes longer than expected—a delayed staff meeting, a slow elevator—he immediately assumes something bad is happening, that the universe is about to spring another trap. He cannot relax, even at home, which he knows is safe; his body stays braced for impact. The trouble falling asleep began within weeks of the crash and has only worsened, because the moment he closes his eyes, the film starts playing again. The more he relives the event, the more convinced he becomes that he is broken, and the more dangerous the world feels.

Arthur has developed strategies to manage this unbearable state, though each one makes things worse. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts, a mental effort that leaves him exhausted and hollow, and which secretly confirms to him that he must be deeply damaged if he has to work this hard just to feel normal. He has also started eating excessively in the evenings, a habit that has added fifteen pounds and now makes him feel ashamed and out of control. The most consequential strategy, however, is his avoidance of work. As a principal, his days were filled with sudden loud noises—slamming doors, fire drills, a child shouting in the hallway—and every shout, every bang, every unexpected crash yanks him back into the crash. He began taking sick days, then medical leave. He has not set foot in the school in six weeks. His assistant principal calls with questions; Arthur stares at the phone and lets it ring. Each day he does not go in, he tells himself that a real principal would have handled this, that he is a coward, that he has permanently changed for the worse. The world is dangerous, he is broken, and the only way to survive is to stay still, to stay quiet, to stay home.

But staying home has not helped. In the silence, his mind replays the crash. The more he replays it, the more he feels its immediacy, and the more he feels the world closing in. A delivery truck backfiring on his street sends him to the floor. His wife found him there last week, and she insisted he call someone. Arthur is here now because he is afraid of what he is becoming—a man who cannot work, cannot sleep, cannot even answer his own front door without his chest seizing. He is hoping, though he barely dares to say it aloud, that someone can help him find a way back to the person he used to be.
